title: Sleep in school‐age children at elevated familial likelihood of autism
abstract: Abstract Background Clinically significant sleep problems are common in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and can have negative impacts on child cognition, behavior, and health. However, few studies have evaluated sleep in school‐aged children with elevated familial likelihood of autism using objective and subjective sleep measures in the home environment. Methods We obtained objective measures of sleep using actigraphy and parent‐report of sleep problems using daily sleep diaries and the Children's Sleep Habits Questionnaire. Direct assessment established ASD diagnosis in 7‐14‐year‐old children at higher familial likelihood (HL‐ASD n = 39; HL‐noASD n = 83) and lower familial likelihood of ASD (LL n = 64). Results Child sleep problems reported by parents, controlling for age, differed across groups following an endophenotypic pattern (HL‐ASD > HL‐noASD > LL) and HL‐ASD females demonstrated increased sleep problems. Actigraphy and daily sleep diaries did not demonstrate significant group differences. There were significant group differences in psychotropic medication and melatonin use. Conclusion In one of the first studies to evaluate sleep in school‐age children at higher familial likelihood of ASD, parent‐report of sleep problems was increased in HL‐ASD versus HL‐noASD versus LL children. This suggests shared familial influences between ASD and parent‐reported sleep problems which could include genetic factors or shared aspects of the home environment. However, sleep characteristics measured objectively by actigraphy and daily sleep diaries revealed a different pattern. Multimodal sleep data can reveal less understood dimensions of sleep patterns in naturalistic home environments and may lead to improved sleep interventions for autistic youth and their siblings.
